title: SIGIL Hash-Chained Agent Communication Protocol
filing_authority: MEOK Sovereign Substrate (SOV3) — IP-First AI Operating System
abstract: A hash-chained agent communication protocol (SIGIL — Sovereign Inter-agent Grounded Interaction Ledger) that provides cryptographically provable message ordering, integrity verification, and authenticity attestation for multi-agent AI substrates operating without central coordination. Unlike traditional agent communication protocols (FIPA-ACL, A2A Agent-to-Agent Protocol, MCP, IPC) that rely on centralised message brokers, trusted third parties, or pairwise TLS, the SIGIL protocol implements a distributed hash chain where each inter-agent message includes a cryptographic hash of all prior messages in the conversation thread, creating a tamper-evident sequence. The protocol operates at three layers: Layer 1 (SIGIL Chain) provides a linear hash chain linking successive messages with SHA-256 hashes, signed by the sending agent's Ed25519 keypair; Layer 2 (SIGIL Council) provides BFT quorum attestation of message ordering for critical coordination decisions, with >=22/33 council nodes signing each consensus round; Layer 3 (SIGIL Anchor) provides periodic anchoring of the chain hash to a public Solana devnet ledger for long-term tamper-evidence and third-party verification. Each message carries a SIGIL header containing: (i) the chain identifier and sequence number; (ii) the hash of the previous message in the chain; (iii) the sender's Ed25519 public key; (iv) the sender's Ed25519 signature over (chain_id || seq || prev_hash || message_hash); (v) optional council quorum signatures for Layer 2 attestation; and (vi) the anchoring transaction ID for Layer 3 commitments. The protocol supports branching (concurrent conversation threads) and merges (council-mediated intent resolution) through a DAG-aware variant, with an off-chain verifier that can validate any SIGIL chain given only the genesis anchor and the ordered messages.

claims.claim: A hash-chained agent communication protocol (SIGIL) comprising: (a) a linear hash chain at Layer 1 linking successive inter-agent messages via SHA-256 hashes, signed by each sending agent's Ed25519 keypair; (b) a BFT council attestation mechanism at Layer 2 providing quorum-verified message ordering for critical coordination decisions, requiring >=22/33 council node signatures; (c) a periodic anchoring mechanism at Layer 3 committing the chain hash to a public blockchain ledger for long-term tamper-evidence; and (d) an off-chain verifier that can validate the integrity and ordering of any SIGIL chain given only its genesis anchor and ordered message sequence.

The protocol of claim 1, wherein each message carries a SIGIL header comprising: chain identifier; sequence number; hash of previous message in chain; sender Ed25519 public key; sender Ed25519 signature over (chain_id || seq || prev_hash || message_hash); optional council quorum signatures; and anchoring transaction identifier for Layer 3 commitments.

The protocol of claim 1, further comprising a DAG-aware variant that supports branching and merging of conversation threads through a directed acyclic graph structure, with branch reconciliation mediated by the BFT council using a plurality voting rule weighted by each agent's reputation score from a sovereign AI substrate.

The protocol of claim 1, wherein the off-chain verifier can detect message reordering, insertion, deletion, or modification by recomputing the hash chain from the genesis anchor and comparing against the attested chain state, with any discrepancy producing a verifiable proof of tampering that can be submitted to the Layer 2 council for adjudication.

novelty_distinction: All prior agent communication protocols (FIPA-ACL, A2A, MCP, SOAP, gRPC-AI) lack cryptographically verified message ordering — they rely on transport-layer ordering (TCP, TLS) or central coordinators that are opaque to third-party verification.
Hash chains for message ordering have been used in messaging apps (Signal's Sesame, Keybase) but only for pairwise conversations — not for multi-agent BFT council attestation with public anchoring.
The three-layer architecture (chain + council + anchor) is novel — existing systems use at most two layers (application message + transport cryptographic protection).

The DAG-aware branching and merging with reputation-weighted reconciliation is novel in the context of multi-agent AI systems, enabling concurrent workstreams within a single provable conversation graph.
